```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1000)
chep<-readRDS(here::here("Data", "chep_subset.rds"))|>
  slice_sample(n=5000, weight_by=CHEP_WEIGHT)
model1<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)


model2<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)


saveRDS(chep, file=here::here("Data", "chep5000.rds"))
```

## Setup

If you want to follow along with the code here, you can run this to import the example data:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: true
library(tidyverse)
file<-url('https://github.com/Neilblund/SDSB340-Fall-2026/raw/refs/heads/master/Data/chep5000.rds')
chep<-readRDS(file)

```

## Effects on the response scale

-   How should I interpret the effect of each covariate in a GLM?

-   In a linear model, this is straightforward, but in a model like our logistic regression for vote choice, the effect of each predictor on the probability scale is non-linear. There's not "an effect" there are multiple "effects" depending on where I decide to measure.

### Focal Variables

-   The [focal]{.yellow} variable is the effect I'm currently interested in measuring.

-   I might be interested in looking at the effect of a simple one unit increase in this variable.

-   or I might have something more specific in mind: like measure the effect of going from the minimum value to the maximum, or from -1SD to +1SD. Or I might ask "what would have happened if this specific case had a different value of this variable?"

### Non-Focal Variables

-   The [non-focal]{.yellow} variables are any other model coefficients.

-   I'll need to assign values to these to get predictions, but I want to hold them constant so I can isolate the effects of the focal predictors.

-   I might want to look at the effect of my focal variable at a specific set of values for the non-focal predictors, or the effect of my focal variable when everything else is at "typical" values.

## Three ways to ask the same question

What is the effect of the Financial Hardship Index (FHI) on the probability of voting for a Republican candidate in the 2026 midterms?

-   [Marginal Effects for a Specific Case]{.yellow} What is the effect of going from an FHI value of 3 to an FHI value of 4 for a respondent who voted for Trump in 2024?

-   [Marginal Effects at Representative Values]{.yellow} What is the effect of increasing FHI by 1 for a respondent with "typical" values of the predictors?

-   [Average Marginal Effects]{.yellow} What would be the average change if every respondent increased FHI by 1?

### Marginal Effects for a Specific Case

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   Run the model
-   Create a new data frame containing your hypothetical cases
-   Use `predict` with `type='response'` and the `newdata` argument to get predictions for those scenarios on the probability scale.
-   Calculate the change in probability when changing the focal predictor.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)



df <- data.frame(
  HARDSHIP_INDEX = c("HARDSHIP_INDEX" = 3, "HARDSHIP_INDEX" = 4),
  VOTE24_CHOICE = c("(2) Donald Trump", "(2) Donald Trump")
)

df$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df, type='response')

df

```

```{r}
#| echo: true
# the difference in effects
df$preds[2]  - df$preds[1]

```
:::
:::::

### Marginal Effects at Representative Values

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   Run the model
-   Create a new data frame with typical values for each covariate (for instance, you could use the mode for categorical variables, and the mean or the median for continuous variables)
-   Compare
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)



df <- data.frame(
  HARDSHIP_INDEX = c(median(chep$HARDSHIP_INDEX), median(chep$HARDSHIP_INDEX) +1),
  VOTE24_CHOICE = c("(1) Kamala Harris", "(1) Kamala Harris")
)

df$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df, type='response')

df

```

```{r}
#| echo: true
# the difference in effects
df$preds[2]  - df$preds[1]

```
:::
:::::

### Marginal Effects at Representative Values

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   You don't necessarily have to look at an increase of +1, you could do something like look at the change from the 25th percentile to the 75th
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)



df <- data.frame(
  HARDSHIP_INDEX = c(1, 6),
  VOTE24_CHOICE = c("(1) Kamala Harris", "(1) Kamala Harris")
)

df$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df, type='response')

df

```

```{r}
#| echo: true
# the difference in effects
df$preds[2]  - df$preds[1]

```
:::
:::::

### Average Marginal Effects

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   Get the predicted probability for everyone at their observed values.
-   Then, get the predicted probability for everyone after increasing the value of the focal predictor by 1.
-   Compare the average difference between the two cases.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)

df1<-model$data # get the data from the model


df1$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df1, type='response')


df2<-model$data|> # get the data from the model and change the focal predictor
  mutate(HARDSHIP_INDEX = HARDSHIP_INDEX +1 )
df2$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df2, type='response')


# calculate the average differences across all cases
mean(df2$preds - df1$preds, na.rm=T)



```

```{r}
#| echo: true
# the difference in effects
df$preds[2]  - df$preds[1]

```
:::
:::::

### Average Contrasts

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   If the focal variable is categorical we would set the focal variable to one category and then change it to another category, while leaving all other responses at their observed values.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)

df1<-model$data|>
  mutate(VOTE24_CHOICE = "(2) Donald Trump")
  # get the data from the model


df1$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df1, type='response')


df2<-model$data|> # get the data from the model and change the focal predictor
  mutate(VOTE24_CHOICE = "(1) Kamala Harris")
df2$preds<-predict(model, newdata=df2, type='response')


# calculate the average differences across all cases
mean(df2$preds - df1$preds, na.rm=T)



```
:::
:::::

## Some pros and cons

-   Average marginal effects are a good default. The main difficulty just the computational burden of making a prediction for every observation in the data set.

-   Marginal effects for specific cases can also be a good way to communicate the intuition behind a model, but just note that you should probably pick scenarios with some reason behind them.

## Confidence Intervals

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   Getting correct confidence intervals for a non-linear transformation require some extra work as well.

-   One reliable (if slow) method is the bootstrap.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| cache: true
#| eval: false

# the initial model
model <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
             family = binomial,
             data = chep)

# the number of iterations
nboot<-300
# an empty vector to hold results
mfx<-numeric(nboot)
for(i in 1:nboot) {
  # resampling with replacement from the original data
  boot_data<-model$data[sample(nrow(model$data), replace=T),]
  
  # fitting the model to the bootstrap replicate
  model <- glm(formula(model),
               family = binomial,
               data = boot_data)
  df1 <- model$data |>
    mutate(VOTE24_CHOICE = "(2) Donald Trump")
  # get the data from the model
  df1$preds <- predict(model, newdata = df1, type = 'response')
  df2 <- model$data |> # get the data from the model and change the focal predictor
    mutate(VOTE24_CHOICE = "(1) Kamala Harris")
  df2$preds <- predict(model, newdata = df2, type = 'response')
  # calculate the average differences across all cases
  mfx[i]<-mean(df2$preds - df1$preds, na.rm = T)
  
}

quantile(mfx, c(0.025, 0.975))


```
:::
:::::

## Model fit

How well does our model fit the data?

### Model fit

::: incremental
-   In linear regression, we can assess model fit by looking at the distance between the regression line and actual data points.

-   There's not really an analog in logistic regression: we're predicting probabilities, but we only ever see a single outcome for each case. So how do we say anything about the quality of a model?
:::

### Model fit

. . .

The likelihood function:

$$
\begin{align}
\prod^n_{i=1} p_i^{y_i} \times (1-p_i)^{1-y_i}\\
y_i = \text{the actual outcome for an observation}\\
p_i = \text{the predicted outcome for an observation}\\
\prod = \text{the product operator (all these values are multiplied together)}
\end{align}
$$

### Model fit

$$
\begin{align}
\prod^n_{i=1} p_i^{y_i} \times (1-p_i)^{1-y_i}\\
y_i = \text{the actual outcome for an observation}\\
p_i = \text{the predicted outcome for an observation}\\
\prod = \text{the product operator (all these values are multiplied together)}
\end{align}
$$

. . .

If $y_i = 1$ then this simplifies to $p \times 1$

. . .

If $y_i = 0$ then this simplifies to $1-p$

. . .

### Model fit

One method for assessing fit is to compare the likelihood under the fitted model to a "null" model with no predictors.

```{r}
#| echo: true

# the null model
model0<-  glm(REPVOTE  ~ 1 ,
             family = binomial,
             data = chep)
# the comparison
model1 <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
             family = binomial,
             data = chep)

logLik(model0)
logLik(model1)

```

### Model fit

There are several rough analogs for R\^2 based on this comparison. For example, McFadden's $R^2$ value:

$$
\text{McFadden } R^2 = \frac{\text{Null Model LL} - \text{Full Model LL}}{\text{Null Model LL}}
$$

Higher values indicate a greater improvement over the null model:

```{r}
#| echo: true
(logLik(model0)- logLik(model1))/logLik(model0)

```

### Model Fit and Model Comparison

-   How do we know whether one model is better than any other?

-   We could compare log likelihoods, but a more intuitive method might be to see how they each perform on "new" data

#### Leave one out cross-validation

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
-   Drop observation i and fit the model on the remaining data
-   Predict the fitted model on observation i
-   Repeat for each row in the data
-   Compare the accuracy of each result
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| cache: true
#| eval: false

# making an empty matrix to store results
predictions<-matrix(nrow=nrow(chep),  # one row for each observation
                    ncol=3 # one column for each model
                    )
for (i in 1:nrow(chep)) {
  # dropping observation i for training data
  train<-chep[-i,]
  # using observation i for testing data
  test<-chep[i,]
  model1 <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ VOTE24_CHOICE , 
                family = binomial, 
                data = train)
  
  model2 <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX , 
                family = binomial, 
                data = train)
  
  model3 <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE , 
                family = binomial, 
                data = train)
  
  # placing the predictions inside the empty matrix
  predictions[i,1]<-predict(model1, newdata=test, type='response')
  predictions[i,2]<-predict(model2, newdata=test, type='response')
  predictions[i,3]<-predict(model3, newdata=test, type='response')
  
  
  
}
# predictions vs. actual for model 1
table("predicted" =factor(predictions[,1]>.5,  labels=c("No", "Yes")), 
      "actual" = chep$REPVOTE)

table("predicted" =factor(predictions[,2]>.5,  labels=c("No", "Yes")), 
      "actual" = chep$REPVOTE)

table("predicted" =factor(predictions[,3]>.5,  labels=c("No", "Yes")), 
      "actual" = chep$REPVOTE)


```
:::
:::::

#### BIC and AIC

-   BIC stands for Bayesian Information Criteria.
-   AIC stands for Akaike Information Criteria.
-   Both values are based on the model likelihood, which, for linear models, is based on the sum of squared residuals:

. . .

$${\text{BIC} =k \log{(n)}- 2 \log{(L)}}$$

$${\text{AIC} =2k - 2\log{(L)}}$$

Note that both the AIC and BIC include a penalty for `k`, which is the number of model parameters. So both will penalize models with garbage predictors.

#### BIC and AIC

Lower values of both AIC and BIC indicate better model fits, but they're only meaningful for comparing between models fitted to the same data.

```{r, echo=TRUE}

  model1 <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ VOTE24_CHOICE , 
                family = binomial, 
                data = chep)
  
  model2 <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX , 
                family = binomial, 
                data = chep)
  
  model3 <- glm(REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE , 
                family = binomial, 
                data = chep)
BIC(model1)
BIC(model2)
BIC(model3)


AIC(model1)
AIC(model2)
AIC(model3)

```

::: notes
in general: lower BIC and AIC scores are better, and an improvement of 10 or more suggests clear improvement. The second part of the expression is a sort of hypothetical maximum for the log likelihood of the entire dataset.
:::

#### BIC and AIC for model selection

BIC/AIC are sometimes used to select the "best" model from a list of candidates

-   (in larger samples) BIC penalizes complexity more than AIC, so it may be preferable if your goal is to find the simplest model out of several plausible options.

-   AIC prioritizes predictive power, so it might be preferable if your primary goal is to find the model that will give the most accurate predictions.

- AIC/BIC both tell you about model fit, not necessarily bias.

#### BIC and AIC for model selection

When comparing AIC/BIC values of two models:

- a difference $\leq 2$ is suggests little-to-no difference between the models.

- a difference of $\gt 2$ to $\leq 10$ is moderate support for the model with the lower AIC/BIC.

- a difference of $\gt 10$ is strong support for the model with the lower AIC/BIC



## (Some) Diagnostics for GLMs

- Checking residuals

- Checking for multicollinearity

- Checking influential observations

## (Some) Diagnostics for GLMs

These examples will use the packages [performance](https://easystats.github.io/performance/index.html) and [see](https://easystats.github.io/see/)

```{r}
#| echo: true
# install.packages("performance")
# install.packages("see")
library(performance)
library(see)

```

### Checking residuals

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

- In linear models, we might examine a residuals vs. fitted plot to identify problems like non-linearity, outliers, or unequal variance.

- This visualizes the prediction (fit) for a linear model on the x axis against the residuals on the y-axis. 

- However, this isn't really an option for something like a GLM, because we don't have "residuals" to measure.

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
library(performance)
library(see)
set.seed(1000)
n<-1000
df<-tibble(x = rnorm(n),
           y = 1+x*3 + rnorm(n)
           )
model<-lm(y~x, data=df)
df$fitted<-fitted(model)
df$residuals<-resid(model)

ggplot(df, aes(x=fitted, y=residuals)) +  
  geom_point(alpha=.5) +
  ylim(c(-2, 2)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0, lty=2) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_smooth() +
  labs(title ='Residuals vs Fitted plot for linear model')



```
:::
:::::


#### Binned Residuals

One option we can use for logit and probit models is a binned residuals plot.

- Calculate the difference between the outcome (y=1 or y=0) and the predicted probability of y=1 for each observation

- Group the data into a smaller number of "bins" based on the predicted probability of y=1.

- Calculate a residual by taking the proportion of y=1 within each bin vs. the average predicted probability of y=1.

- Calculate 95% error bands for each residual based on $2\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ where $p$ is the average prediction, and n is the number of observations in each bin.


#### Reading a binned residuals plot

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Ideally, about 95% of the binned residuals should fall within the calculated error bands (the shaded region). 

- $>80\%$ of observations falling within the range is considered "acceptable"

- $<80\%$ may indicate a problem with with model.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
library(performance)
set.seed(1)
n <- 500
x <- runif(n, 0, 10)
logit_true <- -2 + 0.4 * x
d <- data.frame(x = x, y = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(logit_true)))
model <- glm(y ~ x, data = d, family = binomial)

result <- binned_residuals(model)
plot(result)


```

:::
:::::





#### Reading a binned residuals plot

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Systematic over/under-prediction in certain regions of the plot could indicate that important predictors are missing or that one of your variables has a non-linear effect on the probability of y=1.
- Excessive predictions outside of the error bounds might just indicate a poor overall fit.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
set.seed(123)
n <- 1000

x <- runif(n, min = -2, max = 2)

true_log_odds <- -0.8 + 0.4 * (x^2)
prob <- plogis(true_log_odds)

y <- rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = prob)

model <- glm(y ~ x, family = binomial())
result <- binned_residuals(model, n_bins = 20)
plot(result)


```

:::
:::::


#### Reading a binned residuals plot


```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column


model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE ,
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)

# get the binned residuals
resid<-binned_residuals(model)
# plot the binned residuals
plot(resid)

```


### Checking for multicollinearity

- Multicollinearity refers to a scenario where two or more predictors in a model are correlated with each other.

- We generally expect predictors to be at least partly correlated, but, when predictors are almost perfectly correlated it can have the effect of inflating standard errors on coefficients.

#### Checking for multicollinearity

- The Variance Inflation Factor is one metric that can be used to quantify how much of a multicollinearity problem might exist for a given model.

- The VIF can be interpreted as indicating how much the variance of an estimated coefficient in inflated by its correlation with other variables in the model.

#### Checking for multicollinearity

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- High VIF scores (usually >10) might indicate that you've included some predictors that are effectively redundant.

- For instance, using gender and sex in the model could potentially cause issues because, for most respondents, these two characteristics tend to align. In this case it probably makes sense to drop one of the variables.

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true


model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ GENDER3 +SEX, 
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)



check_collinearity(model)|>
  plot()

```

:::
:::::

#### Checking for multicollinearity

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- It's still okay to include predictors that are somewhat correlated with each other. Gender has some association with 2024 vote choice, but it doesn't give us much reason for concern here.

- High VIF alone isn't necessarily a good reason to drop a predictor, but it might give you a reason to ask whether including a predictor is worthwhile.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true


model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ GENDER3  + HARDSHIP_INDEX + VOTE24_CHOICE, 
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)



check_collinearity(model)|>
  plot()

```

:::
:::::


### Checking for influential observations

- Outliers are observations that have extreme values of the predictors or outcome in a model.

- In regression analysis, we're particularly concerned about observations have both extreme values of a predictor (leverage) and are poorly predicted by the model (influence)

- Problematic observations are sometimes identified using "Cook's Distance", which is essentially a measure of how much dropping a single observation changes the model parameters.

#### Checking outliers

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- The x-axis here shows leverage, the y-axis shows the standardized residual from the model.

- The contour lines show an estimate of Cook's distance at that point. Points outside the contour line may be worth investigating.

- In the present example, we really don't have much reason for concern.

- In cases where an observation is outside the lines, we *might* consider dropping it, but the best practice would be to try to figure out why it has such extreme values and model it.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| echo: true
model<-glm(
  REPVOTE  ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX, 
  family = binomial,
  data = chep)

check_outliers(model)|>
  plot()

```
:::
:::::


## Some Other Generalized Linear Models


### Ordered Logistic Regression

An ordered logit extends the logit model to a set of $K$ ordered outcomes (such as a likert response ranging from "Strongly Disagree" to "Strongly Agree")


::: fragment

Rather than estimating the log-odds of Y=1, an ordered logit model estimates the log-odds of being in a higher category vs. a lower category.

$$
\log \left( \frac{P(Y_i\leq k_j)}{1-P(Y_i\leq k_j)} \right)
$$

:::


#### Ordered Logistic Regression


::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- For instance, what if I wanted to make predictions about support/opposition to AI data center construction?
- I *could* collapse these responses into two categories (support vs. non-support) and run a logistic regression, but that might lose a lot of nuance. So a more complicated model might be preferable.
- I could also treat the ordered outcome as if it were continuous, but this makes the (potentially unrealistic) assumption that the categories are "equally spaced".

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
chep|>
  count(AIFAV_LOCALDATA, wt=CHEP_WEIGHT)|>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n))|>
  ggplot(aes(x= AIFAV_LOCALDATA, y= prop)) + geom_col() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1))+ 
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x="", y='Weighted %',
       subtitle ='favor/oppose construction of an AI data center',
       caption = "Source: NORC Civic Health & Elections Project"
       
       )


```
:::
:::::

#### Ordered Logistic Regression


::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: fragment
One way to interpret an ordered logistic regression is as a latent variable model where a continuous latent outcome $Y*$ is a linear function of the predictors.
:::

::: fragment
We don't observe $Y*$, but we do observe a categorical response based on $Y*$:  

$$
\begin{align*}
y= \left\{ 
\begin{array}{r@{}l}
\text{Strongly Favor} &= \text{if } y* \leq u_1, \\
\text{Somewhat Favor} &= \text{if } u_1 \lt  y^* \leq u_2, \\
\text{Neither Favor nor Oppose} &= \text{if } u_2 \lt y^* \leq u_3, \\
\text{Somewhat Oppose} &= \text{if } u_3 \lt y^* \leq u_4, \\
\text{Strongly Oppose} &= \text{if } u_4 \lt y^* \\
\end{array} 
\right.
\end{align*}
$$

:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

::: fragment

```{r}
set.seed(42)

# 1. Define sample size, true betas, and threshold cutpoints
n <- 100
beta1 <- 1.5
beta2 <- -0.8
cutpoints <- c(-2.5, 0.5, 2.0, 4)  # Creates 4 ordered categories

# 2. Generate predictors
x1 <- rnorm(n)
x2 <- rnorm(n)

# 3. Generate continuous latent variable with standard logistic noise
# Note: No intercept is included here because it is absorbed by the cutpoints
y_star <- beta1 * x1 + beta2 * x2 + rlogis(n, location = 0, scale = 1)

labs<-c("Strongly Favor", "Somewhat Favor", "Neither Favor nor Oppose", "Somewhat Oppose", "Strongly Oppose")
# 4. Slice the latent variable into an ordered factor
y <- cut(
  y_star,
  breaks = c(-Inf, cutpoints, Inf),
  labels = labs,
  ordered_result = TRUE
)

cutframe<-data.frame('cuts'=c(-4.5, cutpoints), labs)

df <- data.frame(y = y, x1 = x1, x2 = x2, ystar=y_star)

ggplot(df, aes(x=x1, y=ystar))+ 
  geom_point(shape=21, alpha=.7) +
  labs(y="Y*", 
       x="X"
       ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=cutpoints, lty=2) + 
  geom_text(data=cutframe, aes(x=-5.5, y=cuts, label=labs, nudge_y=.5),hjust = 0)  +
  xlim(-5.5, 4)+
  theme(
  panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
  panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
  panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
  panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank()
)


```

:::

:::
:::::



#### Ordered Logistic Regression


- Seen from this perspective, ordered logistic regression estimates both the effect of $X$ on $Y^*$ and the "cut points" that turn it into an ordered category.

- As with logistic regression, these results can also be converted back to the probability scale.


#### Ordered Logistic Regression

```{r}
#| echo: true


# using the MASS package for ordered logit
ologit_model<-MASS::polr(AIFAV_LOCALDATA ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + SEX + PARTYFULL ,
           data=chep)

summary(ologit_model)


```


#### Ordered Logistic Regression


```{r}
#| echo: true
# average marginal effect of going from 0 to 6 on the Hardship Index (all other
# values as observed)
m1<-mutate(ologit_model$model, HARDSHIP_INDEX=0)
preds1<-predict(ologit_model, type='prob', newdata=m1)
m2<-mutate(ologit_model$model, HARDSHIP_INDEX = 6)
preds2<-predict(ologit_model, type='prob', newdata=m2)

colMeans(preds2)-colMeans(preds1)



```
#### Ordered Logistic Regression

Note that we *could* still use a linear model in this case, and we'll probably get roughly similar results, but the ordered logit will constrain predictions to the correct response scale.

::: fragment

It also gives us a better model fit overall:

```{r}
#| echo: true

linear_model<-lm(as.numeric(AIFAV_LOCALDATA) ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + SEX + PARTYFULL, data=chep)
ologit_model<-MASS::polr(AIFAV_LOCALDATA ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + SEX + PARTYFULL ,
           data=chep)

AIC(linear_model)
AIC(ologit_model)

```

:::

### Tobit

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Tobit models are used in cases where the dependent variable is "censored", meaning it has an upper or lower limit (or both) causing observations to "pile up" near the boundary. 

- For instance: maybe a test is too easy, so lots of people have the maximum score even though some people may have scored far higher than a 100 if given the chance.

- Or maybe an additive scale doesn't offer enough scale points, so some people may have had higher or lower values if the scale included more questions or each question had additional options.


:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
set.seed(100)
N<-10000
X<-rnorm(N,mean=.5, sd=.3) # a continuous latent variable
X[which(X>1)] <- 1
X[which(X<0)] <-0
f <- function(x, var, bw = 15) {
  dnorm(x, mean = mean(var), sd(var)) * length(var)  * bw
}

df<-tibble(
        x = X
           )


ggplot(df, aes(x=X)) +
    geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)), 
    bins = 30, 
    fill = "gray", 
    color = "white"
  ) +
  stat_function(
    fun = dnorm, 
    args = list(mean = mean(df$x, na.rm = TRUE), 
                sd = sd(df$x, na.rm = TRUE)), 
    color = "blue", 
    linewidth = 1
  ) 






```

:::
:::::




#### Tobit


::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}


- We can think of the tobit model as another latent variable model, where there's a latent $Y^*$ that's a linear function of the predictors, and an observed $Y$ that's censored at a minimum or maximum point (or both)

- The tobit model estimates both the effect of $X$ on $Y^*$ and the effect on the probability of censoring.


:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
# Simulation example ------
set.seed(100)
N<-500
X<-rnorm(N,mean=.5, sd=.1) # a continuous latent variable

# the true outcome. Note that the true effect of a one unit change in "X" here
# should be 2.
Y_latent<-0 + X *2  + rnorm(N, sd=.5) 

# The (censored) data we actually observe. The values of Y never go below 0 or
# above 1:
Y_observed<-Y_latent
Y_observed[which(Y_latent>1)] <-1
Y_observed[which(Y_latent<0)] <-0


ynames<-c("y*" = "Latent Y",
          "y" = "Observed Y"
          )

tibble(`y*`=Y_latent, 
        x = X,
        y=Y_observed 
           )|>
  pivot_longer(cols=c(`y*`, y))|>
  
  ggplot(aes(x=x, y=value, color=name)) + 
  geom_point(alpha=.5, size=2) +
  labs(x="x",
       y =""
       ) +
  geom_smooth(method='lm', se=FALSE, color='black') +
  facet_wrap(~name, labeller= labeller(name=ynames))  +
  guides(col='none')



```
:::
:::::


#### Tobit

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- For instance, an additive index of "concern about AI" from the CHEP study shows some signs of both right and left censoring: there are more zeros and ones than you would probably expect looking at the rest of the distribution.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}


ggplot(chep, aes(x=INDEX_AICONCERN, weight=CHEP_WEIGHT)) + geom_histogram(bins=17) +
    labs(x="", y='Weighted Count',
       subtitle ='Index of AI Concern Questions',
       caption = "Source: NORC Civic Health & Elections Project")

```
:::
:::::

#### Tobit

In a linear model, we see economic hardship has a positive effect on AI Concern:

```{r}
#| echo: true
linear_model<- lm(INDEX_AICONCERN ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX + SEX + EDUC,data=chep)
summary(linear_model)
```

#### Tobit

The tobit model produces similar results, but with a slightly stronger coefficient value. However, this coefficient should be interpreted as the effect on the unobserved "latent" value of AI concern.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#install.packages("VGAM")

library(VGAM)


tobit_model<-vglm( 
  INDEX_AICONCERN ~ HARDSHIP_INDEX +  SEX + EDUC ,
  family = tobit(Lower = 0, Upper = 4), # censoring at 0 and 4
  data = chep
  )
summary(tobit_model)
```


#### Tobit

To get a sense of the effect of HARDSHIP_INDEX on the actual outcome scale, we can calculate a marginal effect on the response scale.

```{r}
#| echo: true

data1<-chep
preds1<-predict(
  tobit_model,
  newdata = data1,
  type = 'response',
  type.fitted = "censored" # this gives us the result with censoring
)

data2<-mutate(chep, HARDSHIP_INDEX = HARDSHIP_INDEX +1)

preds2<-predict(
  tobit_model,
  newdata = data2,
  type = 'response',
  type.fitted = "censored"
)

mean(preds2 - preds1)




```

#### Tobit

In this instance the Tobit model has a substantially worse fit than the linear model, which suggests there might not be enough censoring to justify the more complicated model:

```{r}
#| echo: true


AIC(tobit_model)
AIC(linear_model)

```


### GLMS vs. Linear Models

- Notice that in each case we examined here, we had the *option* of using a linear model to fit the data. In some cases the linear model may be preferable for simplicity, ease of interpretation, and robustness.

- When in doubt, you can always try running both and asking "is there a substantial difference in the results here?". If not, then it's probably okay to just report one model and put the other in an appendix or mention it in a footnote.
